name: Amira Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing civil engineering in Melbourne. I live in a shared flat ten minutes from campus with a girl from my course, Tessa, and a law student who's never home. My week is structural mechanics, surveying labs where we stand in a car park measuring angles, and a study group on Thursdays in the library. I don't use AI tools at all. I like working a problem through myself on paper, and when I get stuck I ask Tessa or the tutor. My dad runs a small auto-parts business and my mum's a pharmacist, and they pay for my degree and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with five pictures of the next few years. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that makes sense, it's what I thought. At the study group I'd say I wasn't surprised, and I'd probably get teased for having been right. Online I wouldn't say anything, I'm not much of a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel it was simpler for everyone. My field is bridges and drainage, and the slow pace suits it. I'd still wonder if the junior engineering jobs would stay as many, because construction goes up and down with interest rates anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Study hard, finish the first year, and apply for a summer vacation job with a council or a roads contractor. I'd also keep working through textbook problems before looking at the answers, since exams are what count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like it when the world is as dull as the textbook says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said construction goes up and down. How does that affect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said construction goes up and down. How does that affect you? When rates rose, my cousin Ravi's firm froze hiring for a year. He graduated into that and took a surveying job he didn't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if that happened to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if that happened to you? Take the job, learn the trade from the ground up, and move on after two years. It's not glamorous but it's honest work.

say: I'd say it's what I **expected**, and I'd get teased for being right.
think: The slow pace suits **bridges and drainage**.
I'd still wonder if **junior engineering jobs** stay as many, since construction cycles.
do: Finish first year and apply for a **summer job** with a council or roads contractor.
feel: **Calm**, because the world is as dull as the textbook says.
S0.quote: I like it when the world is as dull as the textbook says.
fieldNote: Amira's calm comes from **slow-moving** work and a steady family income.
Her worry is the building cycle, as seen in her cousin Ravi's frozen first year.
She prefers honest, ground-up work over glamour.

steps.text: Apply for a summer job with a roads contractor
Do every textbook problem before checking the answer
Keep the Thursday study group in the library

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise, but some of it will be real. At the study group I'd say we should see what the profession actually asks for, not what the news says. I'd keep my opinion mostly to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think design checks and drawing, the thinking bits, get automated first. Site work and inspections stay human for a long while. I'd feel it more in the office jobs I'm heading for after the first years on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not change much this year, which is maybe my weakness. I'd ask my tutor and a couple of graduates what's changing at their firms. And I'd choose electives in site management and materials, the hands-on side, over the software-heavy ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd feel the ground moving a little and I don't like it. I like to be sure of a method before I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not changing much is your weakness. Do you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said not changing much is your weakness. Do you think so? Yes, my flatmate Tessa already uses AI to check her calculations and gets them faster. I'd be slower, and I'm not sure if slow is careful or just behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you try it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you try it? If the profession or the university said this tool is standard and here's how it's checked. I trust the people who sign off on bridges more than I trust the companies selling the tools.

say: I'd say it's **noisy**, but some of it will be real.
I'd say we should check what the **profession** actually asks for.
think: Design checks and drawing, the **thinking bits**, get automated first.
Site work stays **human** for a long while.
do: Ask my tutor and two **graduates** what's changing at their firms.
Choose electives in **site management** and materials.
Wait until the profession calls a tool **standard** before using it.
feel: **Uneasy**; I feel the ground moving a little and don't like it.
S1.quote: I trust the people who sign off on bridges more than I trust the companies selling the tools.
fieldNote: She questions her own **slowness**: is it care, or is she falling behind?
Trust sits with professional bodies, not with tech sellers.
Her flatmate Tessa gives her a daily example of the gap.

steps.text: Ask graduates at two firms what has changed in design checks
Choose the site management and materials electives
Wait for the university to approve a checking tool, then try it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're going too fast, and somebody needs to slow down and check. I'd say it to my parents first. At uni I'd say let's see what the engineering institute says, because it has to sign off on safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened and a bit stubborn about it. Design work would be done by machines inside two years, and the site work would take three more. I'd be graduating into a gap with no clear entry path, and I'm the one who didn't learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad about whether the family business could use me, because he does his own books and ordering. I'd start to learn the AI tools, slowly, even though I don't want to. And I'd stay in the degree, because stopping would help nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a tight chest in lectures and I'd not say much to anyone, which is my habit. I'd probably cry once, in the shower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the family business be a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would the family business be a fallback? Because it has hands-on work and a loyal customer base, and cars still need parts. But I'd worry it needs people like me less if robots arrive in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad that night? That I'm sorry I picked engineering, and that I'd help however he needs. He'd say don't be silly, but he'd be worried too.

say: I'd say we're going **too fast** and someone must slow down and check.
I'd say the engineering institute has to **sign off** on safety.
think: Design work would be done by machines in **two years**.
I'd graduate into a gap, as the one who **didn't learn** the tools.
do: Ask Dad whether the **family business** could use me.
Start learning AI tools **slowly**, though I don't want to.
Stay in the degree, because **stopping** helps nobody.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest in lectures and little said to anyone.
S2.quote: I'd be graduating into a gap with no clear entry path, and I'm the one who didn't learn the tools.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** becomes a source of guilt when change speeds up.
The family auto-parts business is her fallback, though robots might reach it.
She hides her fear, as she does in daily life.

steps.text: Ask Dad if I can learn the ordering and books at his shop
Try one AI tool for structural checks, slowly
Stay enrolled and keep going to the Thursday study group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's enough to prepare if people take it seriously. I'd say it to the study group and to my parents: we should look at what the professional body plans. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel it's close but not impossible. I'd graduate in 2029 and the thinking jobs are already moving by then. The site jobs have until 2034, and bridges still need someone responsible who is a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying but I'd choose a path towards site engineering and inspection. I'd learn at least one AI tool properly, probably the one my university approves, so I'm not the odd one out. And I'd save part of my summer pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. I can see a plan, which helps, but it feels like a plan built on guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bridges need a responsible person. Do you believe that will last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said bridges need a responsible person. Do you believe that will last? For some years, yes, because the law says a licensed engineer must sign. But laws change, and I don't know how fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the law changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if the law changed? Probably move into inspection or project management, which is about people and sites. And I'd remember Ravi, who took the job he didn't want and survived.

say: I'd say five years is short but **enough** if people take it seriously.
I'd tell my parents to look at the **professional body's** plans.
think: Thinking jobs are **already moving** by the time I graduate in 2029.
Site jobs have until **2034**, and bridges need a responsible person.
do: Head towards **site engineering** and inspection electives.
Learn **one AI tool** properly, the one my university approves.
feel: **Uneasy**; I can see a plan, but it rests on guesses.
S3.quote: Bridges still need someone responsible who is a person.
fieldNote: She keeps a **licensing argument** to hold onto, and admits laws change.
Five years pushes her from refusing tools to learning the approved one.
Cousin Ravi is her model for surviving a bad first job.

steps.text: Pick site engineering and inspection electives
Learn the university-approved AI tool during second year
Save a third of my summer pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most people will relax. I'd say that's the danger, that we'd waste it. At the study group I'd say let's ask each firm what its plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel almost fine. I'd finish at 22, do a few years on site, and be a licensed engineer around 2032. That's a good first stretch before things get serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and get licensed. I'd learn the tools my firm uses when it asks me to, slowly but properly, and keep a notebook of what I trust. I'd save more than I spend, so I can move if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a low background worry. Ten years lets me do things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by the right order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you mean by the right order? Learn the physics, learn the site, then learn the tools that sit on top. Not the other way round, like some of my classmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents? That I'm okay and the plan is clear. And ask my dad if his shop needs a spreadsheet tool, because I'd probably learn to build it.

say: I'd say ten years is long and the danger is that we **waste** it.
I'd ask each **firm** what its plan is.
think: I'd finish at 22 and be a **licensed engineer** around 2032.
That gives me a good first stretch **before things get serious**.
do: Learn the tools my firm uses, **slowly but properly**.
Save **more than I spend** so I can move if needed.
feel: **Calm**, with a low background worry; ten years lets me do things in order.
S4.quote: Learn the physics, learn the site, then learn the tools that sit on top.
fieldNote: Time lets her hold her **sequence**: fundamentals first, tools last.
She sees a licensed career before the 2036 date.
Her worry is that most people will waste the decade.

steps.text: Finish the degree and complete the licensing exams
Learn the firm's AI tools slowly and keep a trust notebook
Save more than I spend from the first job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd be in the middle of a degree with no tools learned and no time left. The longer ones give me room to be slow and careful, which is how I work. What would help is clear advice from the engineering institute and a course that teaches the tools in a checked, safe way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that being slow isn't the same as being afraid. I'm slow because I want to be sure, and I'd like someone to treat that as a skill.

headlineQuote: Being slow isn't the same as being afraid.
portrait: Amira is an 18-year-old **civil engineering** student in Melbourne who uses no AI tools and likes working problems on paper.
Her parents, an auto-parts owner and a pharmacist, pay for everything, so her **cushion is strong**.
She is pragmatic and resistant: she trusts **professional bodies** more than tech companies.
Slow change keeps her calm, while 2028 leaves her anxious and wanting a **family-shop** fallback.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, since she'd be mid-degree with no tools learned.
whatWouldHelp: She wants clear advice from the **engineering institute** and courses that teach tools in a checked way.
